editorNote: Software is no longer merely what comes in the box. This week it commands its own shows, export ambitions and a multibillion-dollar trade.
morningLine: Software takes center stage while IBM’s junior PC meets the reviewers.

lead.headline: Software Steps Out of Hardware’s Shadow
lead.dek: A multibillion-dollar American trade looks overseas—and a software show makes clear that programs now constitute an industry of their own.
body: The personal-computer business has spent years measuring progress in processors, memory and disk drives. This week the programs themselves claim the marquee. A March 4 report in The Washington Post describes American personal-computer software as a multibillion-dollar business whose firms are looking beyond the domestic boom toward customers overseas.

Two days later, The New York Times filed “The View From a Software Show.” The timing matters: a gathering organized around programs rather than machines signals a trade gaining its own professional rhythm—publishers, dealers, demonstrations and buyers comparing what computers can actually do.

The opportunity comes with friction. Apple, IBM, Commodore, Atari and Britain’s flourishing micro makers divide the market among incompatible formats. Every successful title therefore brings choices about conversion, distribution and support, while buyers must ask whether the software shelf behind a machine is broad enough to justify its price.

Hardware still sets the limits, but software increasingly determines which machine earns desk space. The industry’s next contest will be fought not only over specifications, but over the programs that turn boxes of chips into useful—and entertaining—personal tools.

stories.headline: IBM’s PCjr Arrives to a Skeptical Reception
body: IBM’s home-minded PCjr reaches its retail-launch month carrying the family name, an 8088-class processor, cartridge slots, enhanced color graphics, three-voice sound and a wireless infrared keyboard. The entry configuration is quoted at $669 to $699, while the 128K enhanced model with a disk drive lists for $1,269 before a monitor.

Reviewers find the compromises as conspicuous as the features. Creative Computing examines limits in compatibility and expansion and sharply criticizes the small chiclet-style keyboard. BYTE’s March newsstand lineup also gives the junior machine close attention. IBM has entered the living room, but buyers must decide whether the badge compensates for the awkward keys and a fully equipped price well above the headline figure.

stories.headline: Micro Games Crowd the Chart
body: The RAM/C all-formats chart published by Personal Computer News on March 17 measures sales through March 8, placing it squarely inside this issue week. Chequered Flag leads, followed by Manic Miner, Fighter Pilot, Atic Atac and Scuba Dive—a top five dominated by the lively British home-computer trade.

That chart complicates the American tale of a videogame crash. Dedicated cartridge consoles may be suffering, yet software for programmable micros remains a vigorous retail business. Activision’s H.E.R.O. and FTL’s Sundog: Frozen Legacy also belong to the March 1984 release conversation, though surviving records do not support a precise street day this week.

stories.headline: Industry Seeks Laws Against “Electronic Trespassers”
body: The Videotex Industry Association is pressing state and federal lawmakers for measures against unauthorized computer access. Its claim that electronic trespass costs members millions of dollars each month is an industry estimate, not an independently audited total, but the appeal shows network intrusion moving into commercial and legislative debate.

A March issue of the young publication 2600 meanwhile gives the emerging hacker and phone-phreak culture a printed voice. Together the artifacts capture a widening argument over access, curiosity, property and law. The period sources supply no named crew behind the association’s complaint, and this account offers no access codes or operational instructions.
